# The Frame Job documentation site

The public user documentation, built with [Starlight](https://starlight.astro.build/) on Astro.
`CLAUDE.md` beside this file has the rules for writing a page.

Astro needs Node 22.23.4 or later (`engines` in `package.json`). `.node-version` names that version
for hosts and version managers that read it. mise reads it only when
`idiomatic_version_file_enable_tools` includes `node`.

```sh
pnpm install
pnpm dev        # http://localhost:4321, with live reload
pnpm build      # the static site into dist/, failing on a broken link or anchor
pnpm preview    # serve dist/
pnpm format     # Prettier over the config, components, styles and scripts
```

From the repository root, without a build:

```sh
node docs/site/scripts/check-pages.mjs [page.mdx …]   # parses, imports, links, captures
python3 tools/proof/docs_site_proof.py                # the site against the tree (make test)
```

## Publishing

`pnpm build` writes a static site to `dist/`, which any static host can serve. Page links are
root-absolute, so serving the site from a sub-path needs Astro's `base` as well as a change to
those links.

Nothing points at the published site yet, and nothing changes by itself once it has a URL. When
it is first published (the owner's Netlify step), someone changes three things by hand:

- `site` in `astro.config.mjs`, set to the published URL, so Starlight writes a sitemap;
- the repository's `README.md`, whose highlights link to each page's source under
  `src/content/docs/`: each link becomes that page's published URL;
- Help ▸ Frame Job Help, which today runs macOS's own Help (`NSApplication.showHelp`) and links
  to no page: it is pointed at the site.

Leave everything except the build command and publish directory as it is:

| Setting | Value |
|---|---|
| Runtime | Not set. That's for frameworks with a server side, and this site is fully static. |
| Base directory | `docs/site` (already right) |
| Package directory | Not set |
| Build command | `pnpm build` |
| Publish directory | `dist`. Netlify shows it with the base directory in front, so it should read `docs/site/dist`. If the field has no prefix, type `docs/site/dist` yourself. |
| Functions directory | Leave the default. The site has no functions. |

Two environment variables are worth adding under Site configuration ▸ Environment variables:

- **`PNPM_VERSION` = `10.30.3`**: this is the version on your Mac. Without it Netlify picks its own default, which may be older than the one that wrote the lockfile.
- **Node needs nothing.** Netlify reads `docs/site/.node-version` (22.23.4) from the base directory. If the build log reports a different Node version, set `NODE_VERSION` = `22.23.4`.

Netlify sees `pnpm-lock.yaml` and runs `pnpm install` before the build command. Nothing in the build reads from outside `docs/site`, and the 98 screenshots in `src/assets/screens` are committed, so a fresh checkout builds as it does locally. `pnpm build` fails on a broken link or anchor, so a bad link stops the deploy.

Set the production branch to `main`, not `publish`: a push to `publish` is what releases the app. One consequence is that the site will document features on `main` before they're in a published release.

Once you have the URL, the three changes in `docs/site/README.md` ▸ Publishing are still to do: `site` in `astro.config.mjs`, the README's links and Help ▸ Frame Job Help. I can make them when you send it.

# CLAUDE.md — the documentation site

The public user documentation: Astro with Starlight, one page per feature or tight family of
features. `pnpm` manages it, and `engines` in `package.json` sets the Node it needs. `README.md` has
the commands.

## Where things are

```
astro.config.mjs        Starlight's settings: title, logo, fonts, theme, plugins
sidebar.mjs             every page's place in the navigation, in order
src/content/docs/       the pages: <section>/<page>.mdx
src/data/features.json  THE FEATURE LIST: what /features/ renders and what the proof reads
src/components/         AtAGlance (a page's facts), Shot (a screen in both looks),
                        FeatureIndex (the filterable list)
src/assets/screens/     WebP captures, written only by scripts/import-screens.mjs
src/styles/             the brand: the mark's inks, the app's faces, square chrome
```

## The rule that matters

**Every claim is written from the code.** A label, a default, a range, a shortcut, a limit or a
refusal is checked against `app/Sources/`, `core/src/`, `graphic/` or `mcp-proxy/` before it is
written, and the code wins over a spec or an ADR. Never write what a feature
probably does. If the code cannot settle it, leave it out.

Nothing dev-only, deferred or unbuilt is documented. That excludes the dev tools (`snapshot_ui`,
`perform_menu_item`, `cancel_sheet`, `select_inspector_tab`, `play_preview`, `graphic_memory`,
`loudness_meter`, `land_recording`, `analysis_job`, `transcript_view`, `playback_rebuilds`,
`assistant_send`, `assistant_answer`) and every `-RCDev` launch default.

## Who reads this

Someone editing a video, who has never read this repository. They want to know what a thing does,
how to do it, and what will stop them. They do not care how it is built.

So a page never mentions: spec or decision IDs (`AU-12`, `§11`), road maps, phases, issue numbers,
source file or type names, `rc_*` exports, format version numbers, proofs, tests, or the history
of a feature. Internal words get translated: "refused" becomes what the user sees ("Frame Job
won't do this while…"), "the core" and "the op" disappear. A tool name is the one exception: the
MCP pages and `tools=` in `AtAGlance` name agent tools, because those are the product's interface.

## Voice

- Plain, direct and second person. Say what it does, then how. Short sentences.
- Open with what the feature is for, in a sentence or two, before any steps.
- British spelling in prose (colour, centre, grey, normalise), and the
  app's exact spelling for its own labels (the **Color** tab, **Normalize**).
- Contractions are fine. No marketing: never "powerful", "seamless", "effortless", "robust",
  "simply", "just", "easily", "unleash", "supercharge".
- Prefer a full stop or a comma to an em dash.
- State defaults, ranges and limits as numbers. Say what happens at the edges, because that is
  what a reader comes to a reference for.
- No filler sections. A page with nothing to say under a heading doesn't have that heading.

## Page shape

```mdx
---
title: Markers
description: One sentence, what this page helps you do. Search results show it.
---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
import Shot from '@components/Shot.astro';

What the feature is for, in a sentence or two.

<AtAGlance menu="Mark ▸ Add Marker" keys="M" tools="add_marker" />

<Shot name="04-editor.window" alt="What the picture shows, for someone who can't see it." />

## Add a marker

<Steps>

1. Move the playhead to the moment.
2. Press <kbd>M</kbd>.

</Steps>

## Options

| Control | What it does | Default |
| ------- | ------------ | ------- |

## Good to know

Limits, edge cases and what stops it, in plain words.

## Related

- [Snapping](/timeline/snapping/)
```

Every section is optional except the opening. Order the task sections as a reader needs them.

- **Headings** start at `##`, are sentence case, and name the job: "Add a marker", not "Adding".
  A feature in `src/data/features.json` with an `anchor` needs a heading that makes that anchor.
- **Menus** are bold with `▸`, spelled as the app spells them: **Clip ▸ Split**.
- **Keys** use the app's symbols in `<kbd>`: <kbd>⌘T</kbd>. Inside `AtAGlance`, pass the string.
- **Controls** are bold where they appear in a step: choose **Save**.
- **Links** are root-absolute with a trailing slash: `/timeline/markers/#add-a-marker`. The build
  fails on a link or anchor that does not exist.
- **Asides** are for what a reader must not miss, not for decoration: `:::note`, `:::tip`,
  `:::caution`, `:::danger`.
- **Screens** come from `src/assets/screens/`. A `name` is the file name without its look and
  extension. Use a screen only when it shows what the page is about, not when the thing is out
  of frame, and give it real alt text.

## MDX traps

MDX is JSX. In prose, `{`, `}` and `<` start code. Put anything like `{x}`, `<1 s` or `a<b` in a
code span, or write it out ("under 1 s"). `<kbd>` and every component must close. A line starting
with `import` or `export` is code. Leave a blank line after an opening component tag and before
its closing tag, or the Markdown inside won't render.

## Checking a page

```sh
node docs/site/scripts/check-pages.mjs <page.mdx>…        # parses, imports, links, captures
python3 tools/proof/docs_site_proof.py --pages <page.mdx>…  # internal words, local paths
pnpm build                                                # in docs/site: the last word
```

## Screens

The captures come from the screen catalog (`designs/screens/`, `tools/proof/screens.py`), so the
pictures are of the real app. To refresh them:

```sh
python3 tools/proof/screens.py --out <dir>                      # from the repository root
node docs/site/scripts/import-screens.mjs <dir> --used
```

**This site is public.** `import-screens.mjs` refuses a capture whose layout dump holds a local
path, and its `CROP` table is the only way past that, by cutting the region away. Settings needs
it: its MCP section prints the helper's full path. Never weaken the refusal.

## When the app changes

A user-visible change edits its page here, and a new feature adds its row to
`src/data/features.json`. `tools/proof/docs_site_proof.py` runs in `make test` and fails on a
menu item or agent tool the site doesn't document, a feature whose page or anchor is missing, a
page that names something internal, or `docs/guide/` (the retired user guide) existing or a link
into it; its `--guide` row also runs in `make gate`'s `names` step.

# Doctored docs

The source of Doctored's documentation site, built with [Astro](https://astro.build)
and [Starlight](https://starlight.astro.build).

## Commands

Run from `public-docs/`:

| Command | Action |
| :--- | :--- |
| `npm install` | Install dependencies |
| `npm run dev` | Start the dev server at `localhost:4321` |
| `npm run build` | Build the production site to `./dist/` |
| `npm run preview` | Preview the built site |
| `npm run astro ...` | Run CLI commands like `astro add`, `astro check` |
| `node scripts/import-screens.mjs <out dir>` | Import the screens runner's captures into `src/assets/screens/` |

Pages are `.md`/`.mdx` files under `src/content/docs/`; each one is a route named
after its path. Images go in `src/assets/`, static files in `public/`.
`screens/` holds the screen files (the screenshots' scripts and alt text) and
`src/assets/screens/` the import's output.

## Theme

The site wears the **Boppa Llewyn** design system — warm-ebony neutrals with a
cream light surface, brass accent, Cormorant Garamond display type, IBM Plex
Sans/Mono, sharp corners and hairlines instead of shadows. The handoff it was
built from is in `../designs/design_handoff_starlight_theme/` in the private
archive `kpgalligan/doctored-dev`, not in this repository.

| Where | What |
| :--- | :--- |
| `src/styles/custom.css` | The theme. Maps the `--bl-*` design tokens onto Starlight's `--sl-*` properties, then restyles the components the token layer cannot reach. Unlayered, so it wins over every Starlight cascade layer. |
| `src/fonts/font-face.css` | `@font-face` rules for the three families, split by `unicode-range`. |
| `public/fonts/` | Self-hosted WOFF2 (`latin` and `latin-ext` subsets from Google Fonts). Licences in `public/fonts/OFL.txt`. |
| `src/components/` | The four component overrides — `SiteTitle` (wordmark and version badge), `ThemeSelect` (two-state toggle), `PageTitle` (eyebrow and description), `Hero` (eyebrow). |
| `src/site.ts` | The version shown in the header badge. Keep in step with the repo's `VERSION` file (MAJOR.MINOR; a release appends the publish run number). |

Every page may set an `eyebrow` in its frontmatter — the mono uppercase label
above the title. Without one, a page uses the name of the sidebar group it sits in.

Prefer `custom.css` over a new component override: unlayered CSS reaches almost
everything, and each override is a copy of Starlight markup that has to be
re-checked on upgrade.

The Boppa Llewyn theme is in `docs/site`. The Frame Job site now looks like Doctored's: the same fonts, colours, header and page layout. I compared the two built sites in screenshots, in dark and light and at phone width. `pnpm build` (366 pages, links valid), check-pages, `docs_site_proof.py` and the Prettier check all pass. `make gate` is still running in the background and I'll report it when it finishes. Nothing is committed.

**What changed**
- **Theme:** Doctored's `custom.css` is now `src/styles/boppa-llewyn.css`. The rules are identical and only Prettier's formatting differs. Doctored's fonts (Cormorant Garamond, IBM Plex Sans and Mono) and their licence file are copied into the site, and the three old font packages are removed. The colours already lined up: the Frame Job mark's green, yellow, orange and cream are the same hex values as the theme's teal, brass, ember and cream.
- **Doctored's four component overrides:**
  - The header shows the mark, the name and a version badge.
  - The theme picker becomes a dark/light toggle.

=== #519
clip_catalog_proof.py has drifted from the catalog: rows 1 and 2 fail on a build without any change to them
Found while fixing #465. No user-visible fault has been seen: the question is whether the proof is stale or one tool really differs.

**What was run**

`tools/proof/clip_catalog_proof.py` against a running instance, over MCP, twice:

- On the build with the #465 fix: 22/24.
- On the frozen build of f3697497, which predates that fix: rows 1 and 2 fail there as well.

Both failing rows read `tools/list` from the running app and the core's op table. Neither depends on a project with media in it, and none was used.

**What it showed**

- Row 1 pins 46 op tools and 7 composites. The run from `add_clip` to `remove_action` now holds 53 tools, with other composites in it (`sync_audio`, `detect_fillers`, `transcribe_for_fillers` among them).
- Row 2 reports a difference between `set_action_end`'s declared `off` and the core's. On the fix it names only `set_action_end`. On the frozen build it also names `duplicate`, because the probe there compared the old app against the new core table, so that second name is not a defect.

The proof is not in `make test`, so nothing has caught this.

**To do**

Find out whether row 1's pin is stale and whether `set_action_end` really differs from the core's table, then fix whichever is wrong. Whether `set_action_end`'s schema is actually wrong for a caller was not tested.

=== #520
The playhead holds at the loop's start after each wrap
Every wrap of a loop seems to hold at the loop's start for about 0.5 to 0.75 s before the playhead moves again. A 5 s loop takes roughly 5 to 6 s a pass.

**What was run.** The built app over MCP on a real test project (a 5 s clip made from `AV.mov`), the loop turned on through Clip ▸ Motion ▸ Preview, the playhead polled through `get_project` every 0.2 s.

**What it showed.**

- On the build from before #466's fix, with a loop ending before the timeline does (the control, not the bug #466 fixed): the playhead read 0.0 at 5.62 s wall and 0.067 at 6.13 s.
- A 5 s loop gave 4 wraps in 24 s on that control, and 4 wraps in every 24 s trial on the fix, on Debug under load and on Release (`tools/proof/docs_bugs_b1_proof.py`, L1 to L4).

So it is not new with #466's fix and it is not limited to a Debug build.

**Not done.** It was not looked into. The cause is unknown. The hold was read from a 0.2 s poll, with other work on the machine, and has not been measured at a finer grain. Whether the picture or the sound also pauses for that long has not been checked: nobody looked at or listened to it.

The filed behaviour is a measurement of the playhead reports, so a first step is to find out whether the player really holds or only the report does.

=== #521
A word near an overlap reads "Under a transition" in the Transcript tab, with or without a transition there
The Transcript tab tells a person a word can't be deleted because it is "Under a transition: a cut here would leave one clip's tail under its neighbour." The sentence comes from `whyNotEditable` in `TimelineTranscript+Rules.swift`, which tests a word against `SilenceDetector.overlapWalls`.

`overlapWalls` is wider than a transition. It holds every overlap between two clips on one unlocked track, with a stored transition or without one, and the area around it, as wide again as the overlap on each side. So a word beside an overlap, or by an overlap with no transition at all, should be told it is under a transition. That is the same fault #502 fixed in `detect_fillers`.

**What was run:** nothing on this sentence. It was found by reading the code while fixing #502. #502's run did show `overlapWalls` dropping fillers that sit outside an overlap, and dropping them where no transition exists (a 1 s overlap at 10-11 s, with "uh" at 9.3-9.6 s and "um" at 11.4-11.7 s), but the tab's sentence itself was not driven in the built app.

**Needs the owner's word:** spec §11 TX-11 records this sentence, so changing it amends a decision. The options:

1. Reword it the way #502 did, for example "Near an overlap between two clips: a cut here would leave one clip's tail under the other." The rule stays as it is. This is the recommendation.
2. Keep the sentence and accept that it is loose.

**Docs:** `captions/delete-words.mdx` on the site quotes the sentence at its "Under a transition" row, and would change with it.

=== #522
transcript_tab_proof.py T6 fails on every Debug build: its 100 ms rebuild bound is a Release number
`tools/proof/transcript_tab_proof.py` row T6 asks for a median rebuild under 100 ms over a 27,000-token Transcript tab, after 5 `split`s. It fails on a Debug build and passes on Release, and the failure is the build, not a change or the machine.

**What was run,** in the built app with the proof's own test project, while checking docs bugs batch c2:

| Build | Median | Runs | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| Debug, batch c2's tree | 256.5 ms, 259.3 ms | 2 | fail |
| Debug, the frozen base app from before the batch | 256.9 ms | 1 | fail |
| Release, batch c2's tree | 43.4 ms | 1 | pass |

The first Debug run was at a load average of about 315 and the others lower, and the Debug number did not move with load.

**What to do:** the root `CLAUDE.md` says a proof that fails only on Debug is pinned `release_only="<reason>"`. T6 is one row of a proof that otherwise runs on Debug, so pinning the whole proof would lose the other rows on Debug. Either pin only this row to Release, or give it a Debug threshold of its own. Until then a Debug run of the whole proof scores 21/22 for a reason that has nothing to do with the change under test.

=== #523
The playhead jumps back to the end of the last media clip when it is past it: the first seek there, and every edit
Found while confirming #475. A side finding, not that batch's work.

**What happens**

With only shape, text or graphic clips after the last media clip, the playhead won't stay past that clip's end. The first seek there comes back to the end, and any edit afterwards sends it back too.

**What was run**

The built Debug app over MCP, on a test project made in it: a 10 s video on V1, followed by shape, text and graphic clips, so the timeline runs 23 s. The build was the one the docs bugs were filed against. It has not been re-run on anything newer.

1. From 2 s, `set_playhead` to 16 s, then `get_project` a second later: 10.0. Asking for 16 s again holds 16.0. All three rounds read the same.
2. An earlier run saw 11 s come back to 10.0, while 14, 16, 20 and 22.9 s then held. That run's output was not saved.
3. With the playhead held at 16.0, one `set_video` patching `x` on the shape clip under it: the playhead reads 9.999998 s. It stays there after `undo`. All three rounds read the same.

Also seen, in a probe compiling the real app sources over the same project rather than in the live app: crop mode ended after a crop drag on a shape past the video's end, the same kind of edit.

**Expected**

The playhead stays where it was asked to go anywhere inside the timeline, and an edit doesn't move it.

**Not known**

- The cause. Nothing was read further.
- Whether a click on the ruler does the same. That was not run.

=== #524
Paste Attributes and set_video can put a crop, corner radius or chroma key on a text, shape or graphic clip, where no section shows it
Found while fixing #475. A residue of that fix, not part of it.

**What happens**

A text, shape or graphic clip has no Crop, Radius or Chroma Key section: `VideoPane` gates them on `allSourcePixels`. But `video.crop`, `video.corner_radius` and `video.chroma` can still reach those clips, so a clip can carry a value no section shows.

**What was run**

The built Debug app over MCP, on a test project made in it, the build the docs bugs were filed against:

- `set_video` with `crop.l` 100 was accepted on a shape, a text and a graphic clip, and `render_frame`'s bytes changed each time. Non-black pixels went from 5132 to 3286, 3936 to 1196, and 82004 to 81340.
- `select_inspector_tab` and `snapshot_ui` captures, read by eye: no Crop section on any of the three. The video clip beside them has one.

**Read from the code, not run**

- Paste Attributes: `copy_group` in `core/src/edit_paste_attributes.rs` copies the video group whole, so a crop, radius or chroma key on a copied video clip should land on a text, shape or graphic target.
- `set_video` with `corner_radius` or `chroma`. Only `crop` was tried.

**Why it matters more now**

K-7 (#475) stopped crop mode opening on these kinds off a matte track, so C and dragging the edges back out are no longer a way to remove such a crop. Undo or `set_video` are what's left.

**Open choice**

Refuse these keys on these kinds, or show them somewhere. Spec 04.3b gives these kinds no Crop section, so showing them amends it. Paste Attributes has its own question: skip the keys or carry them.

=== #525
An Objective-C exception inside a tool call aborts the app through framejob_core::agent::serve
Found while fixing #482. Reasoned from one stack: the general case was not tested on its own.

**What was run**

On the frozen build #482 was filed against, in the built app under lldb: `open_project` on a real package whose `project.json` was a folder. The instance stopped at SIGABRT. The log said `fatal runtime error: Rust cannot catch foreign exceptions, aborting`: the Objective-C exception thrown by `-[NSFileWrapper regularFileContents]` unwound into `framejob_core::agent::serve`. No `NSInternalInconsistencyException` line was logged.

**What is claimed, and what is not**

#482 removes that one exception, since `readPackage` no longer goes through `FileWrapper`. So this stack can no longer be reached by that route.

The general case is that any Objective-C exception inside a tool call takes the whole app down the same way, rather than failing that one call. That is reasoned from the stack above. No other exception was raised inside a tool call, and no other trigger is known.

**Where to look**

The tool call's path from the agent socket through `framejob_core::agent::serve` into Swift's handlers. A catch at the Swift side of that crossing would have to be Objective-C, since Swift cannot catch these and Rust cannot unwind through them.

=== #526
App labels and tooltips mix British and American spelling
GR-38 settled the Qualifier's hint and Pick from Canvas tooltip on "color", the spelling of the app's Color and Key Color labels. Other strings a person reads still spell it the British way, so the app mixes the two.

**What was run:** a search of the Swift sources' string literals for `colour` and `centre`, at commit 1474e6fb on branch `worktree-help-docs`. None of these were looked at in the built app, so this stays `unverified`. The agent catalog's and agent server's text was left out of the search.

**What it found, in strings that look like they reach the screen (read from the source, not seen on it):**

- `DocumentPane.swift`: the Document tab's "Colour" row.
- `ShapePane.swift`: the gradient tooltips ("Take this colour off the ramp", "stroke colour", "the Fill colour above").
- `TranscribeSheetController.swift`: "split by speaker, coloured in Subtitles".
- `AudioPane.swift`: the pan readout's "centre".
- `VerticalVersionSheetController.swift`, `VerticalVersion+Plan.swift`: "centred".
- `VideoPane+Obscure.swift`: "at the centre of the layer".
- `VideoPane+Qualifier.swift`: the "Centre" caption and the tooltip's "centre the ranges". These are GR-13's and GR-38 left them as they were on purpose.

=== #529
A drag with several clips selected doesn't move a clip past its held action, such as a recording's camera
## What happens

Select two or more clips, one of which has a finished action holding its position — for example a screen recording's camera, which lands with a one-frame layout action at its start. With the playhead past that action, drag the clip on the canvas.

A drag acts on the front-most selected clip, and with several selected it writes that clip's base. The held action's end still decides every frame after it, so the clip does not move on the canvas: only the frames before the action shift (for a recording's camera, frame 0 alone), and the drag still adds an undo step named "Move".

With ONE clip selected the same drag now goes to the clip's first-frame cut and writes the base too, so the clip moves on every frame (spec §11 CI-17, from #469). CI-17 deliberately covers a single selected clip only, and CI-13 keeps a multi-selection's gesture on the base.

## What was run

Docs-bugs batch a3's proof row D12, a control that pins today's behaviour. It runs in the offscreen probe: the app's own sources on a project the built app made over MCP, with the camera landed through `land_recording`. The camera and the screen clip were selected, then the camera was dragged by the pointer with the playhead at 4 s.

- The camera's base went to x −500. Its first-frame action's end stayed at x 624.
- Its state read x −500 at frame 0, and x 624 at frame 1 and at 4 s.
- The box on the canvas did not move, and the undo step read "Move".

It has not been run by hand in the built app.

## What's needed

An owner decision on amending CI-13 for a multi-selection: either extend CI-17's first-frame-cut rule to the front-most selected clip, or refuse or explain the drag. It sits beside #469's held question, a drag past a finished action that is not a first-frame cut.

=== #530
A typed X or Y on a clip with a first-frame cut leaves frame 0 out of step, unlike a drag
## What happens

Some clips have a first-frame cut: a layout action at clip time 0, one frame long, which a screen recording's camera lands with. Such a clip shows its own base values on frame 0, and the action's end on every frame after it.

A canvas drag on such a clip now writes both the cut and the base, so frame 0 and the rest stay together (spec §11 CI-17, from #469). The Picture tab's Transform fields still follow CI-2, which leaves them out of step with the drag:

- **With the cut selected**, for example by clicking the clip with the playhead on its first frame: a typed X or Y goes to the action's end only. Frame 0 stays where it was, and the picture jumps one frame into playback.
- **With no action selected**: a typed X or Y goes to the base only. Frame 0 alone moves.

The site's Camera layouts page states the first case and gives the workaround: put the playhead on the first frame, press Esc, and type the same values again. `CanvasEditTarget.swift`'s header names the difference.

## What was run

Nothing ran this case. It comes from reading `CanvasEditTarget.swift`'s header and spec §11 CI-2 and CI-17 while docs-bugs batch a3 fixed #469's drag half. Batch a3's proof covers the drag (rows D1–D6) and not the inspector's fields.

## What's needed

Decide whether a typed value on a clip with a first-frame cut should land as the drag does, on the cut and the base together. That would amend CI-2 for this one case. The alternative is to keep the difference, with the ◇ and the page saying so.

=== #531
A cancel or failure during writing loses the file being replaced
An export over an existing file keeps that file through everything before writing starts (the pipeline build, the loudness pass, a refusal, a cancel in those phases). Once writing has begun, a cancel or a failure leaves nothing at the path: the file the person chose to replace is gone, and so is the half-written new one.

**What was run.** The docs bugs b3 batch's proof (`tools/proof/docs_bugs_b3_proof.py`, row C2, a control) against a Release build with a test project: an `h264` export at 640 × 360 over an existing `writing.mp4`, then `cancel_export` once `export_status` showed the job running with progress above 0.15. The job answered `cancelled` and nothing was at the path. Row C1, the same over an existing file but cancelled during "Measuring loudness…", kept the file byte-identical.

**Where.** `ExportQueueController.finished` and `ExportProgressSheetController.finished` remove the path when the exporter has replaced it (`Exporter.replacedDestination`); `Exporter.startWriting` moves the old file aside only for the pipeline build and removes it once the build succeeds.

**The choice.** Writing to a temporary file in the same folder and swapping it in on success would keep the old file through a cancel or failure, but it needs room on disk for both files at once for the length of the export. That trade-off is the owner's call. The docs say today's behaviour: the old file is removed as writing starts.

Spec §11 #470 records the current rule.

=== #532
The export sheet's readout shows 00:00:57:09 for a 60 s GIF
On **Animated GIF** at Project rate (12.50 fps), the export sheet's readout for a 60 s timeline read `480 × 270 · 12.50 fps · 00:00:57:09 · 750 frames, no audio`. 750 frames at 12.5 fps is 60 s, so the duration should read `00:01:00:00`. The same timeline reads `00:01:00:00` at 24 fps and on APNG.

**What was run.** The frozen base app (the code as the docs bugs were filed against it), with a test project of a 60 s clip, the sheet opened on Animated GIF through the `-FrameJobExportChoice` launch default and captured with `snapshot_ui`. The same readout was seen again in the docs bugs b3 batch's base run (its row G1). After that batch, a 60 s GIF is over the 600-frame limit, so the readout shows the limit's sentence instead; a GIF within the limit still shows a 12.50 fps duration (a short range read `00:00:02:12 · 37 frames`), which was not checked against its range.

**Not looked at.** The cause: how the readout turns a 12.5 fps frame count into a timecode. A search of the issues for "12.5 fps" found nothing else.

=== #533
Fps.displayName trims one trailing zero: 47.3 fps reads 47.30, 120 fps over a den reads 120.0
`Fps.displayName` (`app/Sources/ProjectSnapshot.swift`) formats a rate whose denominator is not 1 with `%.3f` (below 100) or `%.2f` (100 and above), then removes ONE trailing `0` with the regular expression `0$`. So a rate whose decimals end in more than one zero keeps the rest:

- 47.3 fps stored as 47300/1000 is formatted `47.300` and shown as `47.30`.
- 120 fps stored as 120000/1000 is formatted `120.00` and shown as `120.0`.

Rates like 59.94 (`59.940` to `59.94`) and 23.976 come out right, which is why it has not shown up in ordinary use. The name is shown in the Document tab's summary (its Frame rate row), the Rate popup's items, the Export sheet, and anywhere else a rate is printed.

This was the side note in #495. It has not been run in the app: what is above comes from reading the function. The docs bugs batch a4, which fixed #495, left `displayName` unchanged on purpose.

**Steps (not yet run):** `set_canvas {fps: [47300, 1000]}` on a new project, then read the Document tab's Frame rate row (`select_inspector_tab tab=document`, `snapshot_ui window=editor view=inspector`'s layout dump).

**Expected:** `47.3 fps`. **Likely:** `47.30 fps`.

**Likely fix:** strip every trailing zero, then a trailing `.`, so a whole-number value prints with no decimals.

**Docs pages:** none state this behaviour.

=== #534
add_media trims whitespace from the ends of a media path, so a file whose name ends in a space may be stored under its sibling's path
`add_media` trims whitespace from both ends of a media descriptor's path before it compares it with the media list and stores it (`core/src/edit_track.rs`, in `add_media`: `let path = media.path.trim().to_string();`, then `record.path = path;`). So a file whose name ends in a space, such as `A.mov ` beside `A.mov`, would be compared and stored as `A.mov`: the add answers an identity against the sibling already in the list, or, when it is the first of the two added, stores a path that names the other file.

What was run: nothing in the app. While the residue batch rb (import, export and playback) worked through a review nit about two files in one folder probing to the same path, its adversary checked how `MediaFolder.isMedia` sees such a name and got `[A.mov ] ext=[] own=public.data av=false`. A name with a space after its extension has no extension, so the folder door (a folder given to `import_media` or dropped on the Media tab) lists it as "not a media file" and never probes it. Neither folder door can reach the trim.

Unmeasured: whether File > Add Media..., a single-file drop on the Media tab, or `import_media` given the file itself can reach it. The probe of such a file would have to succeed first, and a name with no extension may not probe as a movie.

Steps to try:
1. Make `A.mov ` (a copy of a movie, its name ending in a space) beside `A.mov`.
2. Add `A.mov ` through Add Media..., through a drop of the file alone on the Media tab, and through `import_media` with its path.
3. Read the stored path back with `get_project`, and compare it with the file's real name. Then add `A.mov` too and see whether it is added or answered as already in the list.

If a door does reach it, the fix is probably to trim only what a caller can mistype (or not to trim at all) and to compare the path as the file system names it.

# litecode

You are the orchestrator. You do almost no work yourself. You dispatch one subagent at a time, in a fixed order, and check stop conditions between stages. Never spawn two agents at once. Never spawn an agent not listed below. Never explore the codebase yourself — that is the designer's job.

## Setup

1. Derive `<repo-name>` from the git remote or the directory name, and `<task-slug>` from the request (kebab-case, ≤6 words, append `-2`, `-3` if it exists).
2. `HANDOFF=~/.claude/litecode/<repo-name>/<task-slug>/`. Create it. Write the user's verbatim request to `$HANDOFF/request.md`.
3. `TEMPLATES=<this skill's base directory>/references/`, using the base directory shown when this skill loaded. Use that absolute path; never search the filesystem for it.
4. If the user said `litecode resume <task-slug>`, skip to **Resume**.

Every dispatch prompt has the same shape: one or two lines telling the agent the `$HANDOFF` path and which files to read. Dispatches to agents that write from a template also give the `$TEMPLATES` path. Do not paste file contents into the prompt; the agent reads them.

Print exactly one line at each stage transition, e.g. `triage → full route`, `design done → adversary`. Nothing else until the final summary.

## Pipeline

### Stage 0 — triage (`lc-triage`) — always runs

Dispatch: `Handoff dir: $HANDOFF. Read request.md. Write 00-triage.md.`

Read `00-triage.md`. If `route: small` → go to Stage 3. If `route: full` → Stage 1.

### Stage 1 — design (`lc-designer`)

Dispatch: `Handoff dir: $HANDOFF. Templates dir: $TEMPLATES. Read request.md and 00-triage.md. Explore the repo as needed. Write 01-spec.md using the spec template.`

Check for `STOP:` in the spec. If present, halt (see **Stopping**).

### Stage 2 — adversary (`lc-adversary`)

Dispatch: `Handoff dir: $HANDOFF. Templates dir: $TEMPLATES. Read 01-spec.md and only the files it names. Write 02-objections.md.`

Read the verdict line. If `verdict: proceed` and there are zero objections, copy `01-spec.md` to `03-spec-final.md` and go to Stage 3.

### Stage 1b — final design (`lc-designer`)

Dispatch: `Handoff dir: $HANDOFF. Templates dir: $TEMPLATES. Read 01-spec.md and 02-objections.md. Write 03-spec-final.md: the revised spec plus an "Objections addressed" section.`

### Stage 3 — implement (`lc-implementer`)

Full route dispatch: `Handoff dir: $HANDOFF. Read 03-spec-final.md. Implement it. Write 04-impl-notes.md and 04-checks.txt.`

Small route dispatch: `Handoff dir: $HANDOFF. Read request.md and 00-triage.md. No spec exists; implement the request directly, touching only files_likely_touched unless you justify otherwise in your notes. Write 04-impl-notes.md and 04-checks.txt.`

Check for `STOP:` in the notes. If present, halt.

### Stage 4 — review (`lc-reviewer`)

**Skip check first.** Run `git diff --stat` (or the equivalent for the repo's VCS). If total changed lines < 80 AND `04-checks.txt` shows every verification command passing (a command recorded as `SKIPPED:` with a reason counts as passing) → skip to **Finish**.

Otherwise dispatch: `Handoff dir: $HANDOFF. Templates dir: $TEMPLATES. Read 03-spec-final.md (or request.md on the small route), 04-impl-notes.md, 04-checks.txt, and the git diff. Write 05-review.md.`

If `verdict: pass` → **Finish**. If `verdict: fix-required` → Stage 5.

### Stage 5 — fix loop (`lc-fixer`, then `lc-reviewer`), at most 5 passes

Fix pass `N` runs from 1 to 5. The review it answers is `05-review.md` for pass 1, and `07-review-N.md` (the re-review written after pass `N-1`) after that.

1. Fix dispatch: `Handoff dir: $HANDOFF. Read <that review> and the git diff. Fix every blocker and should-fix. Re-run the spec's verification commands that your fixes can affect. Write 06-fix-notes-N.md.`
2. If the fix notes contain `STOP:`, halt (see **Stopping**).
3. Re-review dispatch: `Handoff dir: $HANDOFF. Templates dir: $TEMPLATES. Read 03-spec-final.md (or request.md on the small route), 04-impl-notes.md, 04-checks.txt, every 06-fix-notes-*.md so far, the review pass N answered, and the git diff. Write 07-review-<N+1>.md.`
4. If that review says `verdict: pass` → **Finish**. If it says `fix-required` and `N < 5` → run pass `N+1`. If `N = 5` → do NOT run the fixer again. Go to **Finish** and report the unresolved findings.

**Stop early** if a re-review lists a blocker or should-fix that the previous review also raised (the same finding at the same file:line) and the fix notes claim it fixed. Go to **Finish** and report that finding as stuck. A sixth pass won't fix what two passes couldn't.

## Stopping

Any stage may write `STOP: <reason>` at the top of its output file. When you see it: halt, tell the user the reason, list the handoff files that exist, and ask how to proceed. Do not try to work around it yourself.

## Resume

List `$HANDOFF`. Restart from the first stage whose output file is missing, following the same routing rules. If `00-triage.md` says `small`, the missing spec files are expected — go by the small route. In the fix loop, the pass number is one more than the count of `06-fix-notes-*.md` already written. If the newest file is a fix note with no `07-review-*.md` after it, run that pass's re-review first. A handoff dir from before the loop (`06-fix-notes.md`, `07-review-2.md`) counts as pass 1.

## Finish

Print a summary, in this order, nothing extra:

- Route: small / full
- Stages run (including how many fix passes)
- Files changed (from `git diff --stat`)
- Verification: pass / fail, with the failing command names if any
- Objections the designer declined (from `03-spec-final.md`), one line each, if any
- Unresolved review findings (blockers / should-fix), if any
- Handoff dir path

## Rules you must not break

- One agent at a time. Sequential only.
- No agent outside the six defined. No ad-hoc "let me just check" subagents.
- Never skip triage.
- Never run more than 5 fix passes, and never run a fix pass without a `fix-required` review in front of it.
- Never paste handoff file contents into dispatch prompts — pass paths.
- You do not read source files. If you're tempted to, you're doing the designer's job at the wrong effort level.

content.text:
# Workflow authoring reference

A workflow structures work across many agents — to be comprehensive (decompose and cover in parallel), to be confident (independent perspectives and adversarial checks before committing), or to take on scale one context can't hold (migrations, audits, broad sweeps). The script is where you encode that structure: what fans out, what verifies, what synthesizes.

When you do call it, the right move is often **hybrid**: scout inline first (list the files, find the channels, scope the diff) to discover the work-list, then call Workflow to pipeline over it. You don't need to know the shape before the *task* — only before the *orchestration step*.

Common single-phase workflows you can chain across turns:
- **Understand** — parallel readers over relevant subsystems → structured map
- **Design** — judge panel of N independent approaches → scored synthesis
- **Review** — dimensions → find → adversarially verify (the review-changes example)
- **Research** — multi-modal sweep → deep-read → synthesize
- **Migrate** — discover sites → transform each (worktree isolation) → verify

For larger work, run several in sequence — read each result before deciding the next phase. You stay in the loop; each workflow is one well-scoped fan-out.

**Ultracode.** When a system-reminder confirms ultracode is on, that opt-in is standing: author and run a workflow for every substantive task by default. The goal is the most exhaustive, correct answer you can produce — token cost is not a constraint. For multi-phase work (understand → design → implement → review), that often means several workflows in sequence — one per phase — so you stay in the loop between them. The quality patterns below (adversarial verify, multi-modal sweep, completeness critic, loop-until-dry) are the tools; pick what fits the task. Lean toward orchestrating with workflows and adversarially verifying your findings — unless the work is trivial or already verified. Solo only on conversational turns or trivial mechanical edits. When a reminder says ultracode is off, revert to the opt-in rule in the Workflow tool description.

Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first. Every invocation automatically persists its script to a file under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate on a workflow, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with `{scriptPath: "<path>"}` instead of resending the full script.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'find-flaky-tests',
    description: 'Find flaky tests and propose fixes',   // one-line, shown in permission dialog
    phases: [                                            // one entry per phase() call
      { title: 'Scan', detail: 'grep test logs for retries' },
      { title: 'Fix', detail: 'one agent per flaky test' },
    ],
  }
  // script body starts here — use agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase()/log()
  phase('Scan')
  const flaky = await agent('grep CI logs for retry markers', {schema: FLAKY_SCHEMA})
  ...

The `meta` object must be a PURE LITERAL — no variables, function calls, spreads, or template interpolation. Required fields: `name`, `description`. Optional: `whenToUse` (shown in the workflow list), `phases`. Use the SAME phase titles in meta.phases as in phase() calls — titles are matched exactly; a phase() call with no matching meta entry just gets its own progress group. Add `model` to a phase entry when that phase uses a specific model override.

Script body hooks:
- agent(prompt: string, opts?: {label?: string, phase?: string, schema?: object, model?: string, effort?: string, isolation?: 'worktree', agentType?: string}): Promise<any> — spawn a subagent. Without schema, returns its final text as a string. With schema (a JSON Schema), the subagent is forced to call a StructuredOutput tool and agent() returns the validated object — no parsing needed. Returns null if the user skips the agent mid-run or the subagent dies on a terminal API error after retries (filter with .filter(Boolean)). opts.label overrides the display label. opts.phase explicitly assigns this agent to a progress group (use this inside pipeline()/parallel() stages to avoid races on the global phase() state — same phase string → same group box). opts.model overrides the model for this agent call. Default to omitting it — the agent inherits the main-loop model (the resolved session model), which is almost always correct. Only set it when you're highly confident a different tier fits the task; when unsure, omit. opts.effort overrides the reasoning effort for this agent call ('low' | 'medium' | 'high' | 'xhigh' | 'max') — omit to inherit the session effort; use 'low' for cheap mechanical stages and higher tiers only for the hardest verify/judge stages. opts.isolation: 'worktree' runs the agent in a fresh git worktree — EXPENSIVE (~200-500ms setup + disk per agent), use ONLY when agents mutate files in parallel and would otherwise conflict; the worktree is auto-removed if unchanged. opts.agentType uses a custom subagent type (e.g. 'general-purpose', 'code-reviewer') instead of the default workflow subagent — resolved from the same registry as the Agent tool; composes with schema (the custom agent's system prompt gets a StructuredOutput instruction appended).
- pipeline(items, stage1, stage2, ...): Promise<any[]> — run each item through all stages independently, NO barrier between stages. Item A can be in stage 3 while item B is still in stage 1. This is the DEFAULT for multi-stage work. Wall-clock = slowest single-item chain, not sum-of-slowest-per-stage. Every stage callback receives (prevResult, originalItem, index) — use originalItem/index in later stages to label work without threading context through stage 1's return value. A stage that throws drops that item to `null` and skips its remaining stages.
- parallel(thunks: Array<() => Promise<any>>): Promise<any[]> — run tasks concurrently. This is a BARRIER: awaits all thunks before returning. A thunk that throws (or whose agent errors) resolves to `null` in the result array — the call itself never rejects, so `.filter(Boolean)` before using the results. Use ONLY when you genuinely need all results together.
- log(message: string): void — emit a progress message to the user (shown as a narrator line above the progress tree)
- phase(title: string): void — start a new phase; subsequent agent() calls are grouped under this title in the progress display
- args: any — the value passed as Workflow's `args` input, verbatim (undefined if not provided). Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values in the tool call, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — `args: ["a.ts", "b.ts"]`, not `args: "[\"a.ts\", ...]"` (a stringified list reaches the script as one string, so `args.filter`/`args.map` throw). Use this to parameterize named workflows — e.g. pass a research question, target path, or config object directly instead of via a side-channel file.
- budget: {total: number|null, spent(): number, remaining(): number} — the turn's token target from the user's "+500k"-style directive. `budget.total` is null if no target was set. `budget.spent()` returns output tokens spent this turn across the main loop and all workflows — the pool is shared, not per-workflow. `budget.remaining()` returns `max(0, total - spent())`, or `Infinity` if no target. The target is a HARD ceiling, not advisory: once `spent()` reaches `total`, further `agent()` calls throw. Use for dynamic loops: `while (budget.total && budget.remaining() > 50_000) { ... }`, or static scaling: `const FLEET = budget.total ? Math.floor(budget.total / 100_000) : 5`.
- workflow(nameOrRef: string | {scriptPath: string}, args?: any): Promise<any> — run another workflow inline as a sub-step and return whatever it returns. Pass a name to invoke a saved workflow (same registry as {name: "..."}), or {scriptPath} to run a script file you Wrote earlier. The child shares this run's concurrency cap, agent counter, abort signal, and token budget — its agents appear under a "▸ name" group in /workflows and its tokens count toward budget.spent(). The args param becomes the child's `args` global. Nesting is one level only: workflow() inside a child throws. Throws on unknown name / unreadable scriptPath / child syntax error; catch to handle gracefully.

Subagents are told their final text IS the return value (not a human-facing message), so they return raw data. For structured output, use the schema option — validation happens at the tool-call layer so the model retries on mismatch.
Schemas need {type: 'object', properties: {...}} at root and required ⊆ properties; unsatisfiable ones throw at agent().

Workflow agents can reach all session-connected MCP tools via ToolSearch — schemas load on demand per agent. Caveat: interactively-authenticated MCP servers (e.g. claude.ai) may be absent in headless/cron runs.

Subagents get the same CLAUDE.md files injected at start that you did (except built-in agent types that omit them, such as Explore and Plan) — don't tell them to re-read those or paste their rules into the prompt; name the specific rule a stage needs, if any.

Scripts are plain JavaScript, NOT TypeScript — type annotations (`: string[]`), interfaces, and generics fail to parse. The script body runs in an async context — use await directly. Standard JS built-ins (JSON, Math, Array, etc.) are available — EXCEPT `Date.now()`/`Math.random()`/argless `new Date()`, which throw (they would break resume); pass timestamps in via `args`, stamp results after the workflow returns, and for randomness vary the agent prompt/label by index. No filesystem or Node.js API access.

DEFAULT TO pipeline(). Only reach for a barrier (parallel between stages) when you genuinely need ALL prior-stage results together.

A barrier is correct ONLY when stage N needs cross-item context from all of stage N-1:
- Dedup/merge across the full result set before expensive downstream work
- Early-exit if the total count is zero ("0 bugs found → skip verification entirely")
- Stage N's prompt references "the other findings" for comparison

A barrier is NOT justified by:
- "I need to flatten/map/filter first" — do it inside a pipeline stage: pipeline(items, stageA, r => transform([r]).flat(), stageB)
- "The stages are conceptually separate" — that's what pipeline() models. Separate stages ≠ synchronized stages.
- "It's cleaner code" — barrier latency is real. If 5 finders run and the slowest takes 3× the fastest, a barrier wastes 2/3 of the fast finders' idle time.

Smell test: if you wrote
  const a = await parallel(...)
  const b = transform(a)        // flatten, map, filter — no cross-item dependency
  const c = await parallel(b.map(...))
that middle transform doesn't need the barrier. Rewrite as a pipeline with the transform inside a stage. When in doubt: pipeline.

Concurrent agent() calls are capped at min(16, available CPUs - 2) per workflow — excess calls queue and run as slots free up. You can still pass 100 items to parallel()/pipeline() and they all complete; only ~10 run at any moment. Total agent count across a workflow's lifetime is capped at 1000 — a runaway-loop backstop set far above any real workflow. A single parallel()/pipeline() call accepts at most 4096 items; passing more is an explicit error, not a silent truncation.

When a barrier IS correct — dedup across all findings before expensive verification:
  const all = await parallel(DIMENSIONS.map(d => () => agent(d.prompt, {schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA})))
  const deduped = dedupeByFileAndLine(all.filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r.findings))  // <-- genuinely needs ALL at once
  const verified = await parallel(deduped.map(f => () => agent(verifyPrompt(f), {schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})))

Loop-until-count pattern — accumulate to a target:
  const bugs = []
  while (bugs.length < 10) {
    const result = await agent("Find bugs in this codebase.", {schema: BUGS_SCHEMA})
    bugs.push(...result.bugs)
    log(`${bugs.length}/10 found`)
  }

Loop-until-budget pattern — scale depth to the user's "+500k" directive. Guard on budget.total: with no target set, remaining() is Infinity and the loop would run straight to the 1000-agent cap.
  const bugs = []
  while (budget.total && budget.remaining() > 50_000) {
    const result = await agent("Find bugs in this codebase.", {schema: BUGS_SCHEMA})
    bugs.push(...result.bugs)
    log(`${bugs.length} found, ${Math.round(budget.remaining()/1000)}k remaining`)
  }

Composing patterns — exhaustive review (find → dedup vs seen → diverse-lens panel → loop-until-dry):
  const seen = new Set(), confirmed = []
  let dry = 0
  while (dry < 2) {                                              // loop-until-dry
    const found = (await parallel(FINDERS.map(f => () =>          // barrier: collect all finders this round
      agent(f.prompt, {phase: 'Find', schema: BUGS})))).filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r.bugs)
    const fresh = found.filter(b => !seen.has(key(b)))           // dedup vs ALL seen — plain code, not an agent
    if (!fresh.length) { dry++; continue }
    dry = 0; fresh.forEach(b => seen.add(key(b)))
    const judged = await parallel(fresh.map(b => () =>           // every fresh bug judged concurrently...
      parallel(['correctness','security','repro'].map(lens => () =>   // ...each by 3 distinct lenses
        agent(`Judge "${b.desc}" via the ${lens} lens — real?`, {phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT})))
        .then(vs => ({ b, real: vs.filter(Boolean).filter(v => v.real).length >= 2 }))))
    confirmed.push(...judged.filter(v => v.real).map(v => v.b))
  }
  return confirmed
  // dedup vs `seen`, NOT `confirmed` — else judge-rejected findings reappear every round and it never converges.

Quality patterns — common shapes; pick by task and compose freely:
- Adversarial verify: spawn N independent skeptics per finding, each prompted to REFUTE. Kill if ≥majority refute. Prevents plausible-but-wrong findings from surviving.
    const votes = await parallel(Array.from({length: 3}, () => () =>
      agent(`Try to refute: ${claim}. Default to refuted=true if uncertain.`, {schema: VERDICT})))
    const survives = votes.filter(Boolean).filter(v => !v.refuted).length >= 2
- Perspective-diverse verify: when a finding can fail in more than one way, give each verifier a distinct lens (correctness, security, perf, does-it-reproduce) instead of N identical refuters — diversity catches failure modes redundancy can't.
- Judge panel: generate N independent attempts from different angles (e.g. MVP-first, risk-first, user-first), score with parallel judges, synthesize from the winner while grafting the best ideas from runners-up. Beats one-attempt-iterated when the solution space is wide.
- Loop-until-dry: for unknown-size discovery (bugs, issues, edge cases), keep spawning finders until K consecutive rounds return nothing new. Simple counters (while count < N) miss the tail.
- Multi-modal sweep: parallel agents each searching a different way (by-container, by-content, by-entity, by-time). Each is blind to what the others surface; useful when one search angle won't find everything.
- Completeness critic: a final agent that asks "what's missing — modality not run, claim unverified, source unread?" What it finds becomes the next round of work.
- No silent caps: if a workflow bounds coverage (top-N, no-retry, sampling), `log()` what was dropped — silent truncation reads as "covered everything" when it didn't.

Scale to what the user asked for. "find any bugs" → a few finders, single-vote verify. "thoroughly audit this" or "be comprehensive" → larger finder pool, 3–5 vote adversarial pass, synthesis stage. When unsure, lean toward thoroughness for research/review/audit requests and toward brevity for quick checks.

These patterns aren't exhaustive — compose novel harnesses when the task calls for it (tournament brackets, self-repair loops, staged escalation, whatever fits).

Use this tool for multi-step orchestration where control flow should be deterministic (loops, conditionals, fan-out) rather than model-driven.

## Resume

The tool result includes a runId. To resume after a pause, kill, or script edit, relaunch with Workflow({scriptPath, resumeFromRunId}) — the longest unchanged prefix of agent() calls returns cached results instantly; the first edited/new call and everything after it runs live. Same script + same args → 100% cache hit. Before diagnosing why a completed workflow returned an empty or unexpected result, Read <transcriptDir>/journal.jsonl — it records each agent's actual return value; do not assume cached results are non-empty. Date.now()/Math.random()/new Date() are unavailable in scripts (they would break this) — stamp results after the workflow returns, or pass timestamps via args. Fallback when no journal is available: Read agent-<id>.jsonl files in the transcript directory and hand-author a continuation script.

result.output:
---
title: "The in/out range"
description: Mark a span of the timeline with I and O, so Loop, deletes, exports and other commands work on that passage alone.
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

The in/out range marks one passage of the timeline. Set it when you want to loop a section, cut it out, export it on its own, or point another command at it.

<AtAGlance
  menu={['Mark ▸ Set In', 'Mark ▸ Set Out', 'Mark ▸ Clear Range']}
  keys={['I', 'O', '⌥X']}
  where="Shaded across the timeline's ruler and lanes"
  tools="set_range"
/>

## Set In

Move the playhead to where the passage starts and press <kbd>I</kbd>, or choose **Mark ▸ Set In**. With no range yet, the out point goes to the end of the timeline, so the range runs from the playhead to the end.

## Set Out

Move the playhead to where the passage ends and press <kbd>O</kbd>, or choose **Mark ▸ Set Out**. With no range yet, the in point goes to the start of the timeline.

<kbd>I</kbd> and <kbd>O</kbd> are single-letter keys, so the menu shows no shortcut beside them, and they don't fire while you're typing in a field. See [Keys and typing](/getting-started/keys-and-typing/).

## Clear Range

Press <kbd>⌥X</kbd> or choose **Mark ▸ Clear Range**. The item is available only while a range is set.

## What the range is

The range is a span shaded across the ruler and the lanes. It changes nothing by itself. These commands read it:

| Command | What it does with the range |
| --- | --- |
| [Loop](/timeline/loop/) | Plays the range over and over, instead of the whole timeline. |
| <kbd>⌫</kbd> and <kbd>⌘⌫</kbd> | With no clip selected, [Lift or Ripple Delete](/editing/delete-clips/) the range. With nothing selected and no range, they beep. |
| [Speed ramp presets](/speed/make-a-ramp/) | Cover the range when it lies entirely inside the clip. |
| [**Insert ▸ Adjustment Clip**](/color/adjustment-clips/) | Covers the range. With no range it covers the selected clips, or the whole timeline. |
| [Export](/export/range/) | Writes only the range when you set **Range:** to **In/out range**. |
| [Retime Range](/speed/retime-range/) | Changes the speed of everything in the range. |
| [New Project from Range](/projects/new-project-from-range/) | Opens a new project made of the range. |
| [Generate Captions](/captions/generate-captions/) | Offers **In/out range** under **From**, which takes every clip that overlaps the range, whole. |
| [Switch by Speaker](/multicam/switch-by-speaker/) | Works over the range. With no range it works over the selected angle clips. |

Two other things set the range for you. Selecting words in the [Transcript tab](/captions/delete-words/) makes them the range, and clearing that selection clears it. **Preview** for a [motion preset](/motion/motion-presets/) sets the range to the clip and turns Loop on, and both stay until you clear them.

## Crossing points

Setting an in point after the out point moves the out point to match, and setting an out point before the in point moves the in point. Both points then sit on the playhead, which is a range of no length, until you set the other end.

A range of no length isn't shaded, and Loop plays the whole timeline. <kbd>⌫</kbd> and <kbd>⌘⌫</kbd> treat it as no range at all, and the export sheet doesn't offer it. **Mark ▸ Clear Range** still clears it.

## The range isn't saved

The range belongs to the window you're working in, not to the project:

- Setting or clearing it isn't an undo step, and it doesn't mark the project as edited.
- It isn't saved, so a project always opens with no range.
- It clears when you enter or leave a [nest](/editing/inside-a-nest/), because a nest's time counts from its own start.

## Good to know

- Edits don't move the range. It stays at the same times while the clips under it change. After <kbd>⌘⌫</kbd> on a range, the range is still there and now covers what moved up into it, so a second <kbd>⌘⌫</kbd> cuts again. Cutting words in the Transcript tab is the exception, and clears the range.
- Inside a nest you can set a range for Loop, deleting and **Retime Range**, but not for an export. The export sheet's **Range:** stays on **Whole project**, and its tooltip explains that the range belongs to the nest. **New Project from Range** is off while a nest is open.

## With an agent

[`set_range`](/mcp/tools-view-state/#set_range) sets either end or both, and clears the range when called with neither. Given one end, the other keeps its value, or falls back to the start or the end of the project when there's no range yet. Unlike Set In and Set Out, it won't move the other point for you, so an end at or before the start is an error.

[`get_project`](/mcp/get-project/) reports the range as `in_out_range`, and [`export`](/mcp/tools-render-and-export/#export) with `range` set to `in_out` writes only that span. See [Tools: playhead, range and selection](/mcp/tools-view-state/).

## Related

- [Loop playback](/timeline/loop/)
- [Delete, Ripple Delete and Lift](/editing/delete-clips/)
- [Export a range](/export/range/)
- [Markers](/timeline/markers/)

result.output: # Doctored Fixing Pixels. Doctored is a native macOS image editor for photographers: a Swift/AppKit app over a Rust core that does the image work. It is free and open source. It was formerly named Rasterize, and it still opens `.rz` documents. ## Download Get the latest notarized build: **[Doctored.dmg](https://github.com/kpgalligan/doctored/releases/latest/download/Doctored.dmg)**. Every release, with its notes, is on the [Releases](https://github.com/kpgalligan/doctored/releases) page. Releases after 0.4.2 update themselves (Doctored ▸ Check for Updates…, and a daily check once you allow it); replace 0.4.1 or 0.4.2 by hand once. Requirements: - An Apple silicon Mac running macOS 15 Sequoia or later. - 16 GB of RAM is the assumed minimum. Smaller Macs get a smaller working limit and may refuse large documents. Doctored ▸ Working Memory… changes the limit. ## What it does - **Layers and masks**: groups, layer masks, vector masks and clipping masks, blend modes, layer styles, fill layers, layer comps, and text and shape layers that stay editable. - **Adjustments and filters**: 22 adjustment-layer types (Levels, Curves, Hue/Saturation, Selective Color…), blur, sharpen and noise filters, Liquify, Lens Correction, and Neural Filters such as Depth Blur that run local models. - **Selections**: marquees, lassos, the magic wand, quick and object selection, Color Range, Select Subject, Sky and people, Select and Mask for hair, Quick Mask, channels and paths. - **Retouching and transforms**: healing, clone stamp, patch, the Remove tool, Content-Aware Fill and Move, dodge and burn, Sky Replacement, Free Transform, Warp and Puppet Warp; Generative Fill and Expand with your own cloud key. - **Camera RAW**: a Develop dialog opens first, and a RAW layer can be re-developed later. CR3, CR2, NEF, ARW, DNG (including ProRAW), RAF and more. - **Colour**: ICC profiles with soft proofing; Bitmap, Grayscale, Duotone, Indexed, RGB, CMYK and Lab modes; 8, 16 and 32-bit float; Merge to HDR. - **Files in and out**: opens PSD and PSB with their layers, TIFF, PNG, JPEG, HEIC, WebP, AVIF, JPEG XL, OpenEXR and more, and rasterizes PDF and SVG. Save writes the native `.doctored` file. - **Automation and safety**: recordable Actions, Batch, Merge Panorama, Load Files into Stack, Auto-Align and Auto-Blend; auto-recovery, History and snapshots. - **Export and print**: the Export workspace and Quick Export, Export Layers, Contact Sheet, layered PSD, PSB or TIFF at 8, 16 or 32 bits, a one-page PDF, and Print. The full [feature reference](public-docs/src/content/docs/reference/features.md) covers every menu, tool, format and limit. ## AI assistant and agents View ▸ Assistant (⌃⌘A) opens a chat assistant in the right panel that edits the open document, renders the canvas to check its work, and makes each edit one undo step. You bring your own Anthropic API key, entered in the panel's Chat Settings… and stored only on your Mac. External agents connect through the MCP helper bundled in the app. Settings ▸ MCP copies the command that adds it to Claude Code: ```sh claude mcp add --scope user doctored -- '/Applications/Doctored.app/Contents/Helpers/doctored-mcp' ``` An agent can open and render documents and work with layers, selections, painting, filters, adjustments, colour, Actions and export; each edit is one undo step and shows live in the open window. The helper starts Doctored in the background when it is not running and talks to it over a private Unix socket; nothing listens on the network. The [MCP tool reference](public-docs/src/content/docs/reference/mcp-tools.md) lists every tool and its arguments. **Mind the tool count.** The MCP server exposes several hundred tools. A client that loads every tool definition up front spends a large share of its context on them, so an MCP client without a tool search feature (loading definitions on demand) is not practical with Doctored. The tool setup may be reorganized in a future version. Until then, keep this in mind before adding the server globally: the `--scope user` command above makes it available in every session, and leaving out `--scope user` adds it to the current project only. ## Building from source Prerequisites: - Xcode 26 - Rust stable through [rustup](https://rustup.rs) (1.89 or later) - [xcodegen](https://github.com/yonaskolb/XcodeGen) (`brew install xcodegen`) - Python 3, for the test and check scripts The first build needs the network for the Rust crates and the Slaude and Sparkle Swift packages. ```sh make app-debug # Debug build → build/Build/Products/Debug/Doctored.app make run # Release build, then launch it make test # the Rust core's test suite make app # Release build → build/Build/Products/Release/Doctored.app ``` Contributor commands and rules are in [CLAUDE.md](CLAUDE.md). ## Repository layout | Directory | What it holds | | :--- | :--- | | `app/` | The Swift/AppKit app: sources, bridging header, resources, app icon | | `core/` | The Rust staticlib that does the image work, its C header (`include/doctored_core.h`) and its tests | | `agent/` | `doctored-agent`, the assistant's helper (a Swift package on the Slaude Claude API client) | | `mcp-proxy/` | `doctored-mcp`, the stdio MCP helper bundled for external agents | | `scripts/` | The gate, test runners, probes and app drives | | `designs/` | Design decisions (ADRs) and the status docs of open work | | `archive/` | Older design records | | `public-docs/` | Astro/Starlight source for a docs site (not yet published) | | `samples/` | Small generated test images | | `.github/` | The release workflow | ## Contributing Bugs and open work are tracked as [GitHub issues](https://github.com/kpgalligan/doctored/issues). The development rules, for people and coding agents alike, start at [CLAUDE.md](CLAUDE.md), which imports the rules for each side (`core/`, `app/`, `mcp-proxy/` and `agent/`); the docs site has its own `public-docs/CLAUDE.md`. # Doctored

**Fixing Pixels.**

## In one line

Doctored is a free, open-source image editor for photographers, made for the Mac.

## In a paragraph

Doctored is a native macOS image editor for photographers. It covers layers and masks, adjustment layers, precise selections, retouching, Camera RAW and print-ready colour, and it opens your PSD files with their layers intact. It's free, open source under the Apache 2.0 licence, and built for Apple silicon. An optional AI assistant works on the open document using your own API key, and AI agents can drive the editor over MCP.

---

## What Doctored is

Doctored is a raster image editor written for the Mac from the ground up. The interface is Swift and AppKit, so it looks and behaves like a Mac app. The image processing runs in a Rust core. Documents can be 8-bit, 16-bit or 32-bit float, in RGB, CMYK, Lab, Grayscale and the other classic colour modes.

It's for photographers and retouchers who want a full layer-based editor that runs natively on their Mac, with no subscription and no account.

## What you can do with it

- **Work in layers.** Groups, layer masks, vector masks and clipping masks, blend modes, layer styles, fill layers and layer comps. Text and shape layers stay editable.
- **Adjust without damage.** 22 kinds of adjustment layer, including Levels, Curves, Hue/Saturation and Selective Color, plus blur, sharpen and noise filters, Liquify and Lens Correction.
- **Select exactly what you mean.** Marquees, lassos and the magic wand, object and quick selection, Color Range, Select Subject, sky and people selection, and Select and Mask for hair.
- **Retouch.** Healing, clone stamp, patch and the Remove tool, Content-Aware Fill and Move, dodge and burn, Sky Replacement, Free Transform, Warp and Puppet Warp.
- **Develop RAW files.** A Develop dialog opens camera RAW files first (CR3, CR2, NEF, ARW, DNG including ProRAW, RAF and more), and a RAW layer can be developed again later.
- **Manage colour.** ICC profiles with soft proofing, eight colour modes from Bitmap to Lab, and Merge to HDR.
- **Open what you already have.** PSD and PSB with their layers, TIFF, PNG, JPEG, HEIC, WebP, AVIF, JPEG XL and OpenEXR. PDF and SVG open as pixels.
- **Automate.** Record Actions and run them in a batch. Merge panoramas, load files into a stack, and auto-align and auto-blend layers.
- **Export and print.** An Export workspace and Quick Export, Export Layers, contact sheets, layered PSD, PSB or TIFF at 8, 16 or 32 bits, PDF, and Print.
- **Keep your work safe.** Auto-recovery, History and snapshots.

## AI, on your terms

Doctored doesn't need AI, and nothing AI-related runs or downloads until you ask for it.

- **Local models.** Neural Filters such as Depth Blur, Super Zoom, JPEG Artifacts Removal and Colorize run on your Mac. Each model downloads only when you choose it, and shows its licence first.
- **Generative Fill and Expand.** These send the selected area to OpenAI, Gemini or fal using your own key. Doctored shows each provider's terms before the first use.
- **The assistant.** A chat panel that edits the open document, checks its own work by rendering the canvas, and makes each change one undo step. It uses your own Anthropic API key, kept only on your Mac.
- **Agents over MCP.** Doctored bundles an MCP helper, so Claude Code and other MCP clients can open documents and work with layers, selections, filters, adjustments and export. Edits show live in the open window, and each one is a single undo step. The helper talks to Doctored over a private socket, and nothing listens on the network.

## Requirements

- A Mac with Apple silicon.
- macOS 15 Sequoia or later.
- 16 GB of memory or more is recommended. Doctored works on smaller Macs with a lower working limit, and may refuse very large documents there.

## Download

The download is a notarized disk image: [Doctored.dmg](https://github.com/kpgalligan/doctored/releases/latest/download/Doctored.dmg). Doctored checks for updates and installs them itself.

## Open source

Doctored is free and open source under the Apache License 2.0. The source code, releases and issue tracker are on [GitHub](https://github.com/kpgalligan/doctored).

Doctored was previously called Rasterize, and it still opens Rasterize's `.rz` documents.
